# Compressing the responses generated by learning

2026-09-22. Internally checked theory/design assessment, not promoted material.
No numerical experiment was run. The two companion check reports verify
specified elementary lemmas; they are not fresh independent research or
promotion reviews. A fresh-agent allocation was unavailable, so a reused
agent was restricted to prompt-only verification with no prior scientific
inputs. No earlier study's results enter the arguments below.

## Conclusion and research contract

The strongest candidate identified here is an adaptive hierarchy of forward
and backward response spaces, combined with streaming compression of the
learned middle-weight increment. Its order counts retained directions,
selected by the learning process, rather than derivative degree at
initialization. There is an algebraic approximation theorem for the learned
increment and a causal streaming primitive with a matching bound. There is
not yet a convergence or useful-cost theorem for the combined nonlinear
population solver.

The intended comparison is with the canonical dense flow, with both hidden
layers and the readout trained, at a fixed physical horizon. Relevant errors
are prediction errors and errors in the actual forward and adjoint actions
used to evolve the state. A low-rank approximation of a known trajectory is
not the requested autonomous simulation. A retained dense initial matrix,
an uncharged action oracle, or an unspecified population-field integration
oracle would also fail the full compression requirement.

## 1. Canonical equations and an actual algebraic bound

Use the canonical two-hidden-layer tanh model, with normalized input
\(u=x/\sqrt d\), probability training law \(\mu\), and population
expectations \(\mathbb E_1,\mathbb E_2\). On the circle in the established
source, \(d=2\) and \(u\in S^1\). Set

\[
\begin{aligned}
 H^{(1)}(t,x)&=\tanh(W^{(1)}(t)u),\\
 Z^{(2)}(t,x)&=W^{(2)}(t)H^{(1)}(t,x),\\
 H^{(2)}(t,x)&=\tanh Z^{(2)}(t,x),\\
 f(t,x)&=\mathbb E_2[W^{(3)}(t)H^{(2)}(t,x)],\\
 \Delta^{(2)}(t,x)&=W^{(3)}(t)\operatorname{sech}^2 Z^{(2)}(t,x),\\
 \Delta^{(1)}(t,x)&=\operatorname{sech}^2(W^{(1)}(t)u)
                 (W^{(2)}(t))^*\Delta^{(2)}(t,x).
\end{aligned}
\]

Products of fields here are pointwise. The star is the actual Hilbert-space
adjoint. Write \(r=f-y\), \(W^{(2)}=W_0+K\), with \(K(0)=0\).
For half squared loss \(\mathcal L=\tfrac12\mathbb E_\mu r^2\), the
population equations in canonical mobilities are

\[
\begin{aligned}
 \dot W^{(1)}&=-\mathbb E_\mu[r\Delta^{(1)}u],\\
 \dot K&=-\mathbb E_\mu[r\Delta^{(2)}\otimes H^{(1)}],\\
 \dot W^{(3)}&=-\mathbb E_\mu[rH^{(2)}].
\end{aligned}                                                    \tag{1}
\]

Here \((a\otimes b)v=a\mathbb E_1[bv]\). At finite equal width with RMS
inner products this is the matrix \(ab^\top/n\). The book uses unhalved
loss, whose velocity is twice (1): its trajectory at time \(t\) is this
half-loss trajectory at time \(2t\). The zero initial readout used below
is the limiting population readout, not a claim that the finite random
readout initialization was zero.

Assume the canonical strong flow exists on \([0,T]\), as well as the
measurability needed for these integrals. Let
\(R=\sqrt{2\mathcal L(0)}\). Loss dissipation gives
\(\|r(t)\|_{L^2(\mu)}\le R\). The zero limiting readout and bounded
tanh give

\[
 \|W^{(3)}(t)\|_\infty\le Rt,\qquad
 \|\Delta^{(2)}(t,x)\|_2\le Rt,\qquad
 \|H^{(1)}(t,x)\|_2\le1.
\]

Define the accumulated magnitude of the rank-one updates by

\[
 A(T)=\int_0^T\mathbb E_\mu\!left[
 |r|\,\|\Delta^{(2)}\|_2\,\|H^{(1)}\|_2\right]dt.
\]

The triangle inequality for the trace norm, whose value on a rank-one
operator is \(\|a\|_2\|b\|_2\), proves

\[
 \|K(t)\|_*\le A(T)\le\tfrac12 R^2T^2,\qquad 0\le t\le T.       \tag{2}
\]

More precisely, if \(S(T)=\int_0^T\|r(t)\|_{L^2(\mu)}dt\), then
\(\|W^{(3)}(t)\|_\infty\le S(t)\) and
\(A(T)\le\int_0^T S(t)S'(t)dt=S(T)^2/2\). Neither residual
integrability to infinite time nor a useful numerical value of this bound
is asserted.

Let \(s_j\) be the decreasing singular values of \(K(t)\). Their sum is
at most \(A(T)\). Therefore \((P+1)s_{P+1}\le A(T)\), and truncating
the singular-value decomposition gives

\[
 \inf_{\operatorname{rank} B\le P}\|K(t)-B\|_{\rm op}
 \le\frac{A(T)}{P+1},\qquad
 \inf_{\operatorname{rank} B\le P}\|K(t)-B\|_{\rm HS}
 \le\frac{A(T)}{\sqrt{P+1}}.                                  \tag{3}
\]

For the second inequality, sum
\(\sum_{j>P}s_j^2\le s_{P+1}\sum_{j>P}s_j\le A(T)^2/(P+1)\).
The rank budget and constants do not explicitly depend on width or sample
count (the target scale and horizon matter). These are pointwise-in-time
approximation theorems, not rates for an evolving compressed model.

The operator norm is relevant to network predictions. If the other state
variables are held equal, replacing \(K\) by \(B\) changes the prediction
by at most

\[
 |f_K(t,x)-f_B(t,x)|
 \le\|W^{(3)}(t)\|_2\|K(t)-B\|_{\rm op}\|H^{(1)}(t,x)\|_2.
                                                                    \tag{4}
\]

This follows from Cauchy--Schwarz and the 1-Lipschitz property of tanh.
It is still a same-state comparison; it does not control feedback through
future first-layer or readout updates.

The companion TRACE_BOUND_CHECK.md also verifies one lower subspace of
dimension \(P\) that works uniformly for this entire given trajectory,
with HS error \(A(T)/\sqrt{P+1}\). That subspace uses the full trajectory
up to \(T\) and is an oracle existence result, not the proposed algorithm.

## 2. What this says about the user's structural intuition

Finitely many samples do not imply finite exact rank of the learned
increment: the rank-one factors can rotate through new directions over
time. Even a single sample can generate a span larger than one. The
stronger useful statement here is different: finite accumulated update
magnitude forces summable singular values. Many independent directions
can occur, but they cannot all have a large singular value at a fixed
finite update budget.

The theorem concerns the learned change, not Gaussian initialization.
It does not establish that a universal frozen dictionary captures the large
singular directions economically, that polynomial order sorts them by
importance, or that training always proceeds from low to high Fourier
frequency. Those would be additional claims. It also does not prove that
the observed small-rank approximation is good for any particular task.

## 3. A causal way to retain learned directions

A finite time/data discretization of (1) generates a stream
\(a_j u_j\otimes v_j\), with unit factors and real coefficients.
The factors are the current backward and forward features; the coefficient
includes residual, time increment, sample weight, and factor norms.
They are evaluated at the compressed model's own current state.

One can retain a small operator without retaining all old factors. On
\(\mathcal H_2\oplus\mathcal H_1\), lift each increment to

\[
 z_j=(\sqrt{|a_j|}u_j,
       \operatorname{sign}(a_j)\sqrt{|a_j|}v_j).
\]

The upper-right block of \(\sum_jz_j\otimes z_j\) is exactly the update
sum, and its trace is \(2\sum_j|a_j|\). Retain a PSD rank-\(P\) sketch:
append \(z_j\otimes z_j\); when its rank reaches \(P+1\), subtract its
smallest positive eigenvalue from every positive eigenvalue. This removes
at least one direction. Retained directions consequently merge and rotate
as actual learning responses arrive.

The rule is the covariance form of Frequent Directions. Its complete
elementary proof and our off-diagonal bounds are in
ADAPTIVE_PRIMITIVES_CHECK.md. At every prefix, if \(\widetilde K_N\) is
the sketch's upper-right block,

\[
 \left\|\widetilde K_N-\sum_{j\le N}a_j u_j\otimes v_j\right\|_{\rm op}
 \le\frac{\sum_{j\le N}|a_j|}{P+1},\qquad
 \left\|\widetilde K_N-\sum_{j\le N}a_j u_j\otimes v_j\right\|_{\rm HS}
 \le\frac{\sum_{j\le N}|a_j|}{\sqrt{P+1}}.                       \tag{5}
\]

This is a deterministic pathwise result, including for a stream depending
on the current sketch. No future dense trajectory is accessed. Storage is
\(P\) joint population vectors, or \(O(nP+P^2)\) scalars at width \(n\).
Ordinary repeated hard SVD truncation is not the rule proved here.

Crucial qualifications: the reference sum in (5) is the sum of this
realized stream, not the dense model's updates. Its accumulated weight is
\(\widetilde A_N=\sum|a_j|\); the exact-flow loss bound (2) cannot
automatically be imposed on it. Compression can increase loss. This is
compression of canonical weight updates, not Euclidean gradient descent
on freely trainable factors, which generally induces another weight-space
metric. Convergence of the compressed updates as a discretization of the
original flow is an additional obligation.

## 4. Compressing the initialized operator's required actions

Keeping \(W_0\) as a dense matrix would leave quadratic storage and dense
products. Gaussian \(W_0\) is not globally approximated well in operator
norm by a small rank matrix. Instead retain its action on a growing lower
query span \(V\), and its adjoint action on an upper query span \(U\).
Both query types refer to the same operator.

For finite width let \(W_0\) have iid \(N(0,1/n)\) entries and suppose
the full actions on these spans have been observed. With orthogonal
projectors \(P_V,P_U\), define

\[
 \widehat W_0=W_0P_V+P_UW_0-P_UW_0P_V.                         \tag{6}
\]

It is determined by the retained observations, has rank at most
\(\dim V+\dim U\), and satisfies

\[
\begin{aligned}
 W_0-\widehat W_0&=(I-P_U)W_0(I-P_V),\\
 \|(W_0-\widehat W_0)h\|&\le\|W_0\|_{\rm op}\operatorname{dist}(h,V),\\
 \|(W_0^*-\widehat W_0^*)\delta\|
 &\le\|W_0\|_{\rm op}\operatorname{dist}(\delta,U).
\end{aligned}                                                   \tag{7}
\]

This suggests adding a direction when a required forward or backward query
has too much component outside its retained span. The distances are
computable from the compressed state's own queries, without seeing an
unobserved dense-target trajectory.

There is also an exact finite-Gaussian way to acquire a new action without
storing the unobserved matrix. Conditional on a legitimate sequential query
history, its law is

\[
 W_0\ \stackrel{\rm law}{=}\widehat W_0+(I-P_U)G(I-P_V),          \tag{8}
\]

where \(G\) is fresh iid Gaussian with the same variance, independent of
that history. For each new direction one samples only the needed response
vector and updates the constraints. One does not sample/store a full fresh
matrix, forget old observations, or treat the adjoint as independent.
The proof conditions the unrevealed rectangular Gaussian block; see the
companion report for the adaptive induction. Directions and stopping
decisions must use only previous observations and independent auxiliary
randomness.

The book's Gaussian source/response calculus is the appropriate population
language for this reuse. Its bounded-program results are not by themselves
a proof for a growing-query algorithm, continuous-time limit, or arbitrary
population solver. Equation (8) is asserted here only at finite width and
finite sequential histories.

## 5. The proposed hierarchy and the decisive open step

The proposed state consists of the first-layer and readout populations,
the learned-update sketch, the bidirectional initial-action cache, and
small Gram/coefficient matrices. At finite width, let
\(Q=\dim U+\dim V\). Middle-layer storage is
\(O(n(P+Q)+(P+Q)^2)\), in addition to the first-layer/readout state,
data, and integration work. The approximation has at least two distinct
budgets, \(P\) and \(Q\); only their sum is a defensible retained-direction
count. It is not legitimate to charge only for the small coefficient matrix.

A fixed-rank learned sketch and a response-tolerance cache are concrete
causal primitives. They are not yet a fully analyzed solver. In particular,
the refresh order, time integration, and feedback must be specified for an
implementation; the two exact primitives alone do not fix those choices.

The central conjecture is that on a useful fixed nonlinear horizon, for an
appropriate regular problem class, their own-history combination admits a
bound of the form

\[
 \sup_{t\le T}\|\widetilde f(t,\cdot)-f(t,\cdot)\|_{L^2(\mu_x)}
 \le C_T\left(\frac{A_T^{\rm bound}}{P+1}
       +\varepsilon_{\rm responses}
       +\varepsilon_{\rm time/data/population}\right)^{\alpha_T}, \tag{9}
\]

with explicitly controlled \(C_T,A_T^{\rm bound},\alpha_T>0\), and
with an economical bound on the required query count \(Q\). Equation (9)
is a target, not a proved inequality; even linear dependence
\(\alpha_T=1\) is not asserted. The exact-flow residual bound cannot
substitute for an a priori bound on the compressed evolution.

The next mathematical bottleneck is propagation of the action/update
defects through the fully nonlinear first-layer equation. In particular,
\(\phi'(Z^{(1)})W^*\Delta^{(2)}\) contains a generally unbounded reverse
field. Plain RMS bounds do not give a width-uniform Lipschitz estimate for
products of its perturbation with activation-derivative perturbations.
Reached-state moment/tail control is needed. Established discussion in
finite_optimization_and_controls.md section 13 identifies precisely this
distinction between a supplied-path approximation and autonomous evolution.

Other material obligations are economical own-query growth, no loss of
adjoint consistency, and population-resolution cost. A bounded collection
of population vectors is not automatically a low-dimensional scalar law
or a tractable quadrature. Smoothness of supplied query curves suggests
input/time covers, but does not prove an own-history cache-size bound.
No useful time-uniform theorem or universal small-rank accuracy is claimed.

## 6. Claim ledger and choice of direction

| Claim | Status | Decisive qualification |
|---|---|---|
| Trace-class learned increment with (2) | Proved from canonical equations on an existing flow | Fixed horizon; zero limiting readout; half loss |
| Algebraic rank approximation (3) | Proved | Same-state existence, not autonomous training |
| Fixed lower span for a whole supplied path | Proved in companion report | Uses that entire path |
| Causal streaming bound (5) | Proved for finite streams | Reference is its own realized stream |
| Bidirectional interpolation and posterior (6)–(8) | Proved for finite iid Gaussian matrices | Queries use only recorded history |
| Full compressed trajectory convergence | Open | Nonlinear stability and own-state bounds |
| Useful low-order accuracy / runtime | Open, untested | Must count response cache and population resolution |
| Frozen hierarchies are inherently inefficient | Not established | This study does not test or disprove them |
| Dense learning cannot be compressed | Not established | Increment bound (3) gives a positive structural result |

This is one coherent direction, not several unrelated proposals: choose
the represented directions from forward/backward responses that training
actually produces, and control the error in their actions and accumulation.
It has a more direct importance criterion than derivative order. The
mathematical grounds justify investigating it, not declaring its empirical
or complete theoretical success.
